title: Epicurus, Death, and the Wrongness of Killing
abstract: Abstract This article questions the assumption, held by several philosophers, that the Epicurean argument for death's being “nothing to us” must be fallacious since its acceptance would undermine the principle that killing is (in general) wrong. Two possible strategies are considered, which the Epicurean-sympathizer might deploy in order to show that the non-badness of death (for the person who dies) is compatible with killing's being wrong. One of these is unsuccessful; the other is more promising. It involves arguing that the wrongness of killing is a “basic moral certainty” and hence requires no underpinning by the judgement that death is bad. Problems for this proposal, and possible responses to those problems, are considered. Though the strategy is not decisive, it is deemed to be one that the Epicurean could plausibly adopt. Notes 1. Clearly there will be disagreement about whether some particular instances or kinds of killing are wrong; but the fact that there is room for such disagreement does not invalidate the claim that there is a general norm in place here. 2. Other arguments have been proposed by subsequent Epicureans, most notably Lucretius. Here I will discuss only the argument that occurs in the remains of Epicurus' own writings. For more thorough discussion, see Warren (Citation2004). 3. For the sake of clarity, I have slightly amended the translator's punctuation. 4. See, for example: Silverstein (Citation1993, p. 107); Rosenbaum (Citation1993, pp. 126–27); McMahan (Citation1993, pp. 234–35); and Nussbaum (Citation1994, pp. 201–02). 5. See for example (among many others) Nagel (Citation1993) and Fischer (Citation1997). 6. For critical discussion of Silverstein's views, see Burley (Citation2008) and Silverstein (Citation2008). 7. The view that being dead at a given time precludes one's having a level of well-being at that time has recently been challenged by Ben Bradley: “… I deny that a person must exist at a time in order to have a well-being level at that time” (Bradley, unpublished conference paper; cf. Bradley Citation2009, pp. 98–111). This contention has been disputed by David Hershenov, who argues that, “if death brings non-existence then it is misleading to posit that the dead have zero pleasure …. They are not in a state devoid of pleasures and other goods because they are not in any state at all, hence they can't instantiate or lack anything” (2007, p. 174). I am, roughly, in agreement with Hershenov on this point, although I would stress that what is at issue here is the conceptual question of whether it makes sense to attribute a level of well-being (even a zero level) to a deceased person (as opposed to a metaphysical question about whether non-existent persons can have a state of well-being). 8. McMahan's view of this issue is not straightforward. He says, for example: “Death is not bad in exact proportion to the net amount of good that the life it excludes would have contained. Nevertheless the degree to which death is bad is a function of the value of that life. So to evaluate the badness of a particular death we must have some sense of the value of the life that is lost” (2002, p. 98). For the purposes of my discussion later in this article it is important to note that McMahan's is a deprivationist account of death's badness. Beyond that, however, the precise details need not concern us here. 9. Pleasants has proposed in correspondence (August 2008) that the wrongness of killing be termed a basic moral certainty while the badness of death be termed a basic evaluative certainty. It doesn't appear to me that much hangs on this distinction. 10. Pleasants quotes several examples from the literature, his favourite of which is: “Murder, I suggest, is harmful to its victim because it is an irreversible loss to the person who was murdered of a function or functions necessary for his worthwhile existence” (Levenbook, Citation1984, p. 412; quoted in Pleasants, Citation2008, p. 259). Pleasants regards this as absurd rather than offensive. An anonymous referee has demurred, noting that it is “probably false, but not outrageous”. Personally, I'm in agreement with Pleasants; its absurdity lies in its pretension to say something informative and explanatory while in fact offering a platitude that explains nothing at all. 11. An anonymous referee has proposed, on Pleasants' behalf, that his position need not be equivocal, because perhaps “the badness of death and the wrongness of killing stand or fall together.” But if this were the case, then Pleasants' claim that it is the badness of death that makes killing wrong would have to be balanced by the claim that it is the wrongness of killing that makes death bad. And neither Pleasants nor anyone else wants to be committed to that. 12. It may also be possible for the Epicurean to supply examples of beliefs and values that surround the conviction that killing is wrong, giving it a stable place within our moral framework without appeal to the badness of death. This would, admittedly, be a difficult task, which would require considerable psychological and ethnographical resources. There is not space to attempt it here. 13. In correspondence (August 2008), Pleasants has stated that what he is claiming to be a basic certainty is not that death is bad for the deceased person, but merely that death is bad. If this were the case, then the Epicurean's showing that it is confused to hold that death is bad for the deceased person would not count against Pleasants' proposal. But is the Epicurean not entitled to ask for whom death is bad? Were Pleasants to reply, “Well, I never said it was bad for anyone in particular—it is just bad (simpliciter)”, the Epicurean might then justifiably doubt whether any clear sense has been given to the term “bad” here. 14. Thanks are due to Nigel Pleasants for useful conversation and correspondence on these issues, and to two anonymous referees for helpful and critical comments on an earlier draft. I am also grateful to participants in an ethics seminar at the University of Leeds, where I presented a condensed version of this paper in December 2008, especially my respondent Penny Worth. My research has been assisted by a bursary from the Royal Institute of Philosophy.
